title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction: Setting: let P = 4n+1 be prime. Earlier (Theorem 3 and its corollaries) Euler showed that every number n - q(q+1), or q(q+1) - n, is a quadratic residue mod P. The reason is that 4(n - q^2 - q) = P - (2q+1)^2 ≡ -(2q+1)^2, and -1 is a residue when P ≡ 1 mod 4. Products of residues are residues, and if αβ and α are residues so is β; this led him to conjecture in §13 that every prime factor of these numbers is also a residue mod P. This page continues the numerical test. For P = 73, 89, 97, 101, 109, 113, 137, 149, 157, 173, 181, 193, 197 (cases 9°–21°), with q = 0,1,…,10, Euler lists the absolute values |n - q(q+1)| factored into primes (the row p) and the set r of primes so obtained. He asserts that each such prime is a residue mod P. In §14 (Scholion) he states that this holds in every example. He stresses that it is known only by induction and has no firm proof. On the next page he restricts the claim to the case where 4n+1 is prime and turns it into the 'Conclusio' of §15. In modern terms: if r is an odd prime dividing q^2+q-n, then (2q+1)^2 ≡ P (mod r), so (P/r) = 1. By quadratic reciprocity with P ≡ 1 (mod 4), this gives (r/P) = 1. Conversely, reciprocity for P ≡ 1 mod 4 follows from the conjecture, since any odd prime r with (P/r) = 1 divides some (2q+1)^2 - P. The prime r = 2 occurs exactly when n is even, i.e. P ≡ 1 mod 8, matching the second supplementary law. So the conjecture tested here is equivalent to the quadratic reciprocity law for primes P ≡ 1 (mod 4) together with the 2-supplement. The page is an empirical verification of that law in disguise.
errors: Case 13° (P=109, n=27): at q=7 the value is 56-27 = 29, a prime. The print, as transcribed, gives 3·13 instead, and the r-list accordingly contains 13 and omits 29. But 13 is a quadratic NON-residue mod 109: (13/109) = (109/13) = (5/13) = -1. So, as printed, the table contains a counterexample to Euler's own claim, created by an arithmetic slip. 29 is in fact a residue mod 109. This should be verified against the scan.

Case 19° (P=181, n=45): the value at q=8 is 72-45 = 27 = 3^3. The transcription reads it as 2^2, and the r-list as transcribed contains 2. But 181 ≡ 5 (mod 8), so 2 is a non-residue mod 181, and 2 cannot divide any value since n is odd. If the original really prints 2 in r, it is an error contradicting the claim. Possibly it is only a misreading of the scan.
Case 18° (P=173): the q=0 value n = 43 (prime) is omitted from both the p row and the r row. This is harmless, since 43 is a residue mod 173 (173 ≡ 1 mod 43).
Case 10° (P=89): the last value is 110-22 = 88 = 2^3·11, transcribed as 2^2·11. This may be a print or transcription slip; the r-list is unaffected.

Several exponent slips appear in the transcription, probably OCR rather than Euler: in 11° 24 = 2^3·3, 12 = 2^2·3, 18 = 2·3^2, 32 = 2^5; in 15° 4 = 2^2; in 20° 36 = 2^2·3^2, 8 = 2^3; in 9° 54 = 2·3^3, 72 = 2^3·3^2; in 14° a spurious duplicated 2^2·7. None of these affects the residue claim.
Gap (acknowledged by Euler): the general statement is unproved here. Its proof is equivalent to quadratic reciprocity, first proved by Gauss in 1796/1801.

ideas.what: Conjecture that all prime factors of q^2+q-n are quadratic residues modulo the prime 4n+1, tested numerically on 21 primes
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), plus the second supplementary law, in Euler's 'prime divisors of quadratic forms' formulation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjectured in several forms 1744–1783); Legendre (statement and attempted proof, 1785/1798); Gauss (first proof, 1801)
ideas.where_published: E557 itself (Opuscula analytica I, 1783). Related formulations appear in E552 'Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos' (same volume) and in earlier papers on divisors of x^2+Ny^2. Discussed by Weil (Number Theory: An Approach Through History) and Lemmermeyer (Reciprocity Laws, ch. 1).

ideas.what: Identity 4(q^2+q-n) = (2q+1)^2-(4n+1), linking divisors of the quadratic polynomial with the representations 4p-(2q+1)^2 of the prime
ideas.modern_name: Completing the square / discriminant of x^2+x-n

ideas.what: Observation (on the next page) that the property fails when 4n+1 is composite, e.g. n=11, and is linked to there being exactly n residues for a prime modulus
ideas.modern_name: Jacobi symbol versus quadratic residuosity for composite moduli

missed.claim: Euler's printed verification tables contain at least one arithmetic slip that produces an apparent counterexample to his own claim. For P = 109 he writes 3·13 for 29 and lists 13 as a residue, yet 13 is a non-residue mod 109. Possibly also, for P = 181, he lists 2 as a residue although it is a non-residue. Euler did not notice this while stating that 'all examples' confirm the claim. Whether the Opera omnia editors flagged it is unsure.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is a minor historiographic and editorial point about the reliability of Euler's inductive evidence for reciprocity. It is not new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is numerical evidence for a form of quadratic reciprocity whose Eulerian origin (E552/E557) is well documented by Weil and Lemmermeyer. The only possibly unnoticed detail is the arithmetic slip(s) that place non-residues (13 mod 109, possibly 2 mod 181) in Euler's residue lists.

10°: the last entry corresponds to 88 = 2^3·11 (the print may show 2^2·11).
14°: there are only 11 entries — 2^2·7, 2·13, 2·11, 2^4, 2^3, 2, 2·7, 2^2·7, 2^2·11, 2·31, 2·41 (one 2^2·7 is duplicated in the transcription).
19°: the 9th entry corresponds to 27 = 3^3. The '2^2[?]' is likely a misreading, and the '2' in the r-list should be checked against the scan.
20°: the 4th entry is 2^2·3^2 (36) and the 8th is 2^3 (8).
